<PubmedArticle><MedlineCitation Status="MEDLINE" Owner="NLM" IndexingMethod="Manual"><PMID Version="1">31585085</PMID><DateCompleted><Year>2020</Year><Month>06</Month><Day>09</Day></DateCompleted><DateRevised><Year>2020</Year><Month>10</Month><Day>03</Day></DateRevised><Article PubModel="Print"><Journal><ISSN IssnType="Electronic">1097-4172</ISSN><JournalIssue CitedMedium="Internet"><Volume>179</Volume><Issue>2</Issue><PubDate><Year>2019</Year><Month>Oct</Month><Day>03</Day></PubDate></JournalIssue><Title>Cell</Title><ISOAbbreviation>Cell</ISOAbbreviation></Journal><ArticleTitle>Competing Roles of Slow Oscillations and Delta Waves in Memory Consolidation versus Forgetting.</ArticleTitle><Pagination><StartPage>514</StartPage><EndPage>526.e13</EndPage><MedlinePgn>514-526.e13</MedlinePgn></Pagination><ELocationID EIdType="doi" ValidYN="Y">10.1016/j.cell.2019.08.040</ELocationID><ELocationID EIdType="pii" ValidYN="Y">S0092-8674(19)30959-6</ELocationID><Abstract><AbstractText>Sleep has been implicated in both memory consolidation and forgetting of experiences. However, it is unclear what governs the balance between consolidation and forgetting. Here, we tested how activity-dependent processing during sleep might differentially regulate these two processes. We specifically examined how neural reactivations during non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep were causally linked to&#xa0;consolidation versus weakening of the neural correlates of neuroprosthetic skill. Strikingly, we found that slow oscillations (SOs) and delta (&#x3b4;) waves have dissociable and competing roles in consolidation versus forgetting. By modulating cortical spiking linked to SOs or &#x3b4; waves using closed-loop optogenetic methods, we could, respectively, weaken or strengthen consolidation and thereby bidirectionally modulate sleep-dependent performance gains. We further found that changes in the temporal coupling of spindles to SOs relative to &#x3b4; waves could account for such effects. Thus, our results indicate that neural activity driven by SOs and &#x3b4; waves have competing roles in sleep-dependent memory consolidation.</AbstractText><CopyrightInformation>Published by Elsevier Inc.</CopyrightInformation></Abstract><AuthorList CompleteYN="Y"><Author ValidYN="Y"><LastName>Kim</LastName><ForeName>Jaekyung</ForeName><Initials>J</Initials><AffiliationInfo><Affiliation>Neurology and Rehabilitation Service, San Francisco Veterans Affairs Medical Center, San Francisco, CA, USA; Department of Neurology, University of California, San Francisco, San Francisco, CA, USA.</Affiliation></AffiliationInfo></Author><Author ValidYN="Y"><LastName>Gulati</LastName><ForeName>Tanuj</ForeName><Initials>T</Initials><AffiliationInfo><Affiliation>Neurology and Rehabilitation Service, San Francisco Veterans Affairs Medical Center, San Francisco, CA, USA; Department of Neurology, University of California, San Francisco, San Francisco, CA, USA.</Affiliation></AffiliationInfo></Author><Author ValidYN="Y"><LastName>Ganguly</LastName><ForeName>Karunesh</ForeName><Initials>K</Initials><AffiliationInfo><Affiliation>Neurology and Rehabilitation Service, San Francisco Veterans Affairs Medical Center, San Francisco, CA, USA; Department of Neurology, University of California, San Francisco, San Francisco, CA, USA.
